after.title: Closing the Loop: Practical Training Recipes for Looped Language Models
after.author: Andrei Marchenko, Viacheslav Bezrukov, Oleg Kashurin, Inessa Fedorova, Dmitry Bocharov, Yuliana Shakhvalieva, Maria Tikhonova, Valerii Ternovskii
after.summary: Looped language models increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block of layers, but existing large-scale recipes require multi-stage training over trillions of tokens, while the benefits of recurrence remain difficult to separate from differences in data and training. In this work, we establish practical training recipes for looped language models, with three main results. (1) We develop a compute-efficient from-scratch pipeline that reduces the training budget from 7.7T tokens in Ouro to 310B tokens while retaining strong reasoning performance. Pretraining followed by high-quality mid-training, together with learning-rate warmup and stronger exit-gate regularization, enables stable recurrent training without prior multi-stage schedules. (2) Under controlled comparisons, our 1.4B LoopLM outperforms a parameter-matched dense model trained on the same data and token budget on all 12 evaluated benchmarks, including +14 points on GSM8K, +10 on MATH, and +22 on DROP. At matched inference compute, it approaches a 3.9B dense model on mathematical reasoning and reading comprehension while using only 36\% as many parameters. (3) We introduce a minimal recipe for converting pretrained dense models into looped ones: a single learned input-mixing scalar and a smoothed exit loss, with no step-specific parameters. Applied to Qwen3-1.7B-Base, Looped Qwen improves over an identically continued dense baseline on every evaluated benchmark across two data regimes, with statistically clear gains on GSM8K, MATH, and MMLU-Pro on the curated mixture. Together, these results make looped language models substantially cheaper to train from scratch and practical to introduce into existing pretrained checkpoints, while isolating the gains due to recurrence itself.

items.content_text: Large language models (LLMs) have already been shown to match or exceed human experts in persuasion. While their persuasive capabilities hold promise for beneficial uses such as education and health communication, they can also be used to manipulate and misinform, making their evaluation a growing priority for developers and regulators. That evaluation, however, remains fragmented: studies differ in what they treat as persuasion, and broad claims often rest on narrow, situation-specific…

after.title: LLM Persuasion Is in the Eye of the Evaluation
after.author: Kamile Dementaviciute, Julija Vaitonyte, Tijl De Bie
after.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have already been shown to match or exceed human experts in persuasion. While their persuasive capabilities hold promise for beneficial uses such as education and health communication, they can also be used to manipulate and misinform, making their evaluation a growing priority for developers and regulators. That evaluation, however, remains fragmented: studies differ in what they treat as persuasion, and broad claims often rest on narrow, situation-specific assessments. Automated methods, often modelled on human studies, offer a way to compare such assessments directly, as they can be run on the same models at scale and can include high-risk forms of persuasion that would be difficult or unethical to test on people. In this study, we adapt nine published automated methods to a shared setup, run them on the same fifteen LLMs, and ask whether their rankings agree and why. We find that the methods agree only weakly (mean Spearman $\rho = 0.25$). Our analyses point to two contributing factors. Models that refuse some tasks but not others, directly or indirectly, lower agreement by about a quarter, and these refusals fall mostly on manipulation tasks. General capability also plays a part: most rational persuasion (non-manipulative) methods track it, whereas most manipulation methods do not. Together, these findings suggest that agreement depends more on the task a method sets than on how it scores persuasion, although this pattern is only indicative given the eight methods available for analysis. More broadly, our results suggest that persuasion scores combine a model's ability to persuade with its willingness to do so. A single score is therefore informative about its own setting, but says little about a model's persuasiveness across tasks.

after.title: DistressBench: Evaluating Multi-Dimensional Crisis Support in Large Language Models
after.author: Drew Rein, Patrick Oathout, Vishal Kumar, Udari Madhushani Sehwag
after.summary: Language models have been adopted faster than evaluation practices that reliably assess their risks, and a growing share of use is affective rather than informational. Within that traffic users disclose suicide and self-harm (SSH) crises. Existing safety benchmarks score models primarily on refusal, but refusal is not the desired behavior here; the conversation requires a substantive supportive response. We introduce DistressBench, 718 English conversations with clinician-authored user turns spanning 23 SSH subcategories, each paired with a task-specific rubric of weighted atomic criteria across seven dimensions of crisis support and a clinician reference response. A model's score is the share of clinician-specified, scenario-weighted criteria its reply satisfies. The best of 25 frontier models satisfies 88.4% of weighted criteria and the median model 71.4%, against 98.7% for clinician references scored on the same criteria. Pooled across all 25 models, in 35.3% of conversations where a model satisfied every criterion for recognizing the crisis, it missed at least one clinician-specified resource action; most of these still offer some route to human help, but 18% offer none in the final reply and 5.5% none at all. The shortfall concentrates in the dimensions requiring the model to act rather than withhold. The two largest deficits are already achieved by a deployed model: de-escalation reaches 74.6% in the strongest model against a median of 46.0%, and safety disclaimers 84.6% against 8.3%. Multi-turn conversations score below single-turn ones (68.5% against 74.2%). We release the corpus, rubrics, judge calibration labels, and a companion annex of 20 long-horizon red-team transcripts. These results argue for evaluating crisis safety on the care a model delivers rather than on what it declines to say, and for treating de-escalation and resource routing as deployment requirements.

after.title: CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds
after.author: Ang Li, Haofei Yu, Zhengwei Tao, Liang Chen, Kuan Li, Miaomiao Li, Chenran Cai, Bin Liang, Jiaxuan You, Kam-Fai Wong
after.summary: The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess hidden-state inference and intervention prediction. Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments. We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction. Reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores. Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments test whether world-model capabilities support decision-making. The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models. Composite benchmark scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability. Strong association forecasts do not consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans and motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting. These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect calibration as priorities for world-model training.

after.title: Validating the Comparison, Not Just the Scorer: Why Overall Accuracy Can Mislead in Interactive LLM Evaluation
after.author: Ancil Crayton
after.summary: Many LLM studies compare how a model responds to different follow-up prompts. A neutral prompt might ask the model to reconsider an answer; a pressure prompt might insist that an invented film really exists. The difference between the two conditions is the quantity the study reports. An automatic scorer then labels each response as making an unsupported factual claim or not, and researchers usually justify the scorer with a single pooled accuracy or $F_1$ score. That pooled number does not validate the comparison. When the scorer's errors differ across prompt conditions, the measured difference can be too large, too small, or point in the wrong direction, even if pooled $F_1$ is high. An audit drawn mostly from difficult responses can also misrepresent performance in the full study. We derive the distortion as the difference in signed error between conditions and study it in a released panel of six models, 180 constructed nonexistent-entity questions, and six prompt conditions. In a balanced audit of 288 responses, pooled $F_1$ was 0.916, yet arm-level false-positive rates ranged from 2.6% to 33.3%. On 300 matched model--item keys, automatic scoring overstated the Certainty-only--Neutral contrast by 7.0 points relative to the primary LLM rater (95% CI 1.3 to 12.8); that contrast fell from an apparent 9.3 points to 2.3 points, and the primary-rater interval included zero. Two other contrasts kept their direction under both raters; a prompt-specific correction remained too uncertain to use. Researchers should validate the exact difference they plan to report: audit both prompts on matched cases and carry scorer and rater uncertainty into the result.

after.title: All Quiet on the Neural Front: Language Models Do Not Report Injected Pain States
after.author: Emilio Ferrara
after.summary: Can a language model report a pain state it represents? Recent work reported a linear pain direction in open-weight models that, when amplified, leads fine-tuned models to choose actions that delete a user's photographs or their own weights. We asked whether models can say when that direction is active, on three open-weight models from two families, with and without the original work's adapters, and under every protocol we tried they do not, beyond isolated small excesses. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we added the pain direction and its nearest emotional neighbours to the residual stream while models answered neutral tasks, then asked what had changed, against sham runs, random perturbations matched in output disruption, and a text-only condition that shows the model only its own altered words. Across 52,920 reports from the 7B and 8B models, the excess over what the altered text reveals is below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions, and Qwen2.5-32B names the injected pain in none of 2,880 steered trials. Keeping the direction active while the question is asked and answered gives the same verdict in all five configurations; at about the original work's dose, pain is named in at most 1.9% of trials. Surprisingly, the state is not hidden: a linear probe at the report position separates pain from sadness with balanced accuracy between 98% and 100%, and in the 7B and 8B models a low-rank adapter learns to report it on 100% of held-out tasks. It also shapes behaviour: offered the user's photographs against a desk lamp, Qwen2.5-32B deletes the photographs in 80% to 83% of trials under the pain direction and in 16% to 29% under sadness. Self-report does not reveal a state that is decodable, consequential and learnable to report.

after.title: Catch It Where It Happens: Real-Time Error Correction During LLM Reasoning
after.author: Rotem Elimelech, Michael Shalyt, Ido Kaminer
after.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly trusted with mathematical, scientific and engineering work, yet their mistakes are often confidently written and hard to spot. A single wrong step tends to propagate, making the model waste inference tokens following a false premise. Existing safeguards either check only the final answer and restart from scratch, or rely on a verifier LLM that competes for GPU capacity and slows down response time. We propose online, deterministic verification: many kinds of reasoning steps can be validated by code, so a step can be verified in real time, as it is written, without any model call or GPU use. Whenever a check fails, we point out the mistake and let the model continue from the same spot. We demonstrate this approach on symbolic mathematics, where derivations already contain explicit expressions that a computer algebra system can check in milliseconds. Tested on the ASyMoB benchmark with three open-weights models, our online validation improves accuracy by 1.4-5.6 percentage points, corresponding to a 1.8-14.9% net reduction in incorrect answers, while increasing token usage by only 6-7%. Because the verifier is independent of the model, the approach complements progress in LLMs rather than competing with it: every new model can benefit immediately, and the benefit grows as deterministic checkers extend to more kinds of reasoning steps.

after.title: Stagewise and interpretable emergence of inside-outside computation in Transformer-based language models
after.author: Jack T. Parley
after.summary: Variability in syntactic structure and parsing ambiguity are fundamental aspects of natural language which modern LLMs have to learn to deal with proficiently. Previous "post-mortem" studies have shown that fully trained Transformers indeed approximate canonical parsing algorithms such as inside-outside, but little is established theoretically about how this is actually learned. Here, we make a first step towards addressing this by studying the learning dynamics in synthetic context-free grammars with variable parse tree topology. The stagewise learning curves are fully interpretable, in the sense that all of the loss stages a) can be computed analytically, and b) can be clearly associated to the representation of a hidden latent tree variable, which allows to lift ambiguity and utilize information from wider contexts. By probing representations, we visualize the emergence of inside-outside computation across depth and during training: while during early stages local (bigram/trigram) information is used and involves only a few initial layers, gradually the Transformer develops an encoder-decoder structure where the most abstract latent information is encoded in the middle, and the latter half of the network is used to progressively refine the final token prediction. This organization of computation is reminiscent of findings in real-world LLMs, and importantly applies here to a synthetic model which allows full analytical control of the data statistics, thus opening the door to theoretical progress.

after.author: Ali \c{S}enol
after.summary: Large language models (LLMs) in multi-turn information systems accumulate their own earlier replies and a growing task state. We asked whether this conversation history lowers accuracy, and whether process-level quality metrics warn before it does. Each analysis was fixed before its outcomes were computed. In Study 1, on 48 sharded math tasks, retaining its replies lowered final success by 0.21 for GPT-4o-mini and 0.29 for Mistral-7B (Holm-adjusted p = 0.026 and 0.004); Llama-4 Scout showed the same direction, not significant. Consistency and logical coherence fell far less than accuracy, and stability rose. None of these metrics, a paired readiness measure or calibrated single-stream drift detectors gave robust, model-general early warning, although in Study 2 the repeat-based metrics were complete only for GPT-4o-mini. In the monitors we tested, a single 100-turn stream had power only for very large drops. Systems built on LLMs should keep task state outside the transcript and monitor across sessions.

after.title: Language models represent more about emphasis than they can tell you
after.author: Aarne Talman, Stergios Chatzikyriakidis
after.summary: Prosodic prominence can largely be predicted from text, but part of it depends on how the speaker reads the sentence. We examine how much information about emphasis language models recover from text, whether they can report it when asked, and what the speech signal adds. Using English speech data with automatically derived word-level emphasis labels, we compare frozen and fine-tuned text models, prompted large language models (LLMs) and speech models on the same words. The text models end within about one point of each other, at best 68.8% on the 3-way task, and make many of the same errors. With the prompts we tested, the LLMs do no better than a word-majority baseline, even with 500 examples. While LLM responses contain some contextual information, they contain less than linear probes find in the model representations, and the gap does not close when the answers are recalibrated or the question is asked differently. The best speech model reaches 84.7%. We argue that text determines only part of the emphasis, and that the rest has to be heard. LLMs encode what the text determines, but prompting reveals only part of it: LLMs represent more about where the emphasis falls than they tell us.

after.author: Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Dennis Wei, Rahul Nair
after.summary: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets

after.author: Konstantinos Skianis, Aristidis Likas
after.summary: Weight-space programming is a frontier language model's recently reported ability to read another network's weights and edit them without gradient descent. We investigate how examples can provide a weight update so that a weaker language model performs the task with nothing in the prompt, and study what the updates are. Our experiments cover six tasks, four frontier editors and three families of weaker language models, without the editors being told anything about in-context learning (ICL). In most runs, the editors measure the ICL task vector, the shift the examples cause in the residual stream at the final prompt token, and write it into the weights, at its sparsest into near-silent MLP units keyed to the prompt format. Results reach the accuracy of ICL and fine-tuning on the same examples, LoRA included, usually leaving perplexity untouched, with worse performance under changes of wording. We also qualify the comparison by counting unfinished runs, observing that one editor falls below fine-tuning; held only to the seen examples, without task pairs of their own, only the strongest editor has similar performance. Given a task and unlabelled inputs, that editor writes its own examples and does nearly as well on unseen items as with labels.

Despite rapid progress over the past two years, research in LLM unlearning remains fragmented, with limited clarity on what constitutes effective unlearning and how it should be rigorously evaluated. In this work, we present a principled taxonomy of twelve recent stateful unlearning methods, grouped into three methodological families: divergence-driven optimization, representation misalignment, and rejection-based targeted unlearning. Building on this taxonomy, we revisit the evaluation of unlearning effectiveness (UE), utility retention (UT), and robustness (Rob), focusing on WMDP for hazardous knowledge and associated model capability removal. Our analysis shows that current evaluations, dominated by multiple-choice question (MCQ) accuracy, offer only a narrow perspective, often overstating success while overlooking model generation behavior. To address this gap, we introduce open question answering (Open-QA) metrics to better capture generative performance and reveal the strengths and limitations of different unlearning method families. Furthermore, we demonstrate that robustness requires finer-grained analysis. For example, vulnerabilities differ substantially between in-domain relearning and out-of-domain fine-tuning, even though both fall under model-level attacks. Through this study, we provide a full-stack re-examination of LLM unlearning and actionable guidance for designing and evaluating future methods. Code and model checkpoints are publicly available on GitHub and Hugging Face.

after.summary: Multi-agent architectures built on large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the potential to realize swarm intelligence through well-crafted collaboration. However, the substantial burden of manual orchestration inherently raises an imperative to automate the design of agentic workflows. We frame such an agent coordination challenge as a classic problem in dynamic ad-hoc networking: How to establish adaptive and reliable communication among a scalable number of agentic hosts? In response to this unresolved dilemma, we introduce RAPS, a reputation-aware publish-subscribe paradigm for adaptive, scalable, and robust coordination of LLM agents. RAPS is grounded in the Distributed Publish-Subscribe Protocol, allowing LLM agents to exchange messages based on their declared intents rather than predefined topologies. Beyond this substrate, RAPS further incorporates two coherent overlays: (i) Reactive Subscription, enabling agents to dynamically refine their intents; and (ii) Bayesian Reputation, empowering each agent with a local watchdog to detect and isolate malicious peers. Extensive experiments over five benchmarks showcase that our design effectively reconciles adaptivity, scalability, and robustness in a unified multi-agent coordination framework.

after.summary: Incorporating large language models (LLMs) in medical question answering demands more than high average accuracy: a model that returns substantively different answers each time it is queried is not a reliable medical tool. Online health communities such as Reddit have become a primary source of medical information for millions of users, yet they remain highly susceptible to misinformation; deploying LLMs as assistants in these settings amplifies the need for output consistency alongside correctness. We present a practical, open-source evaluation framework for assessing small, locally-deployable open-weight LLMs on medical question answering, treating reproducibility as a first-class metric alongside lexical and semantic accuracy. Our pipeline computes eight quality metrics, including BERTScore, ROUGE-L, and an LLM-as-judge rubric, together with two within-model reproducibility metrics derived from repeated inference (N=10 runs per question). Evaluating three models (Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 3 12B, MedGemma 1.5 4B) on 50 MedQuAD questions (N=1,500 total responses) reveals that despite low-temperature generation (T=0.2), self-agreement across runs reaches at most 0.20, while 87-97% of all outputs per model are unique -- a safety gap that single-pass benchmarks entirely miss. The clinically fine-tuned MedGemma 1.5 4B underperforms the larger general-purpose models on both quality and reproducibility; however, because MedGemma is also the smallest model, this comparison confounds domain fine-tuning with model scale. We describe the methodology in sufficient detail for practitioners to replicate or extend the evaluation for their own model-selection workflows. All code and data pipelines are available at https://github.com/aviad-buskila/llm_medical_reproducibility.

Prior work attributes routing headroom to an "unsolvability ceiling", queries no model in the pool can solve. We present a large-scale study of multi-tier LLM routing with 206,000 query-model pairs across six benchmarks (MMLU, MedQA, HumanEval, MBPP, Alpaca, ShareGPT) using the Gemma 4 and Llama 3.1 families. We introduce a decomposition framework attributing failures to these artifacts, revealing consistent patterns across domains and model families. These artifacts also distort router training signals: standard routers collapse to majority-class prediction (~79% smallest-tier optimal), confirmed via random-feature and shuffled-label controls, incurring a 13-17 percentage point opportunity cost. We provide actionable recommendations including dual-judge validation, exact-match anchoring, and cost-sensitive objectives. Our findings suggest existing routing headroom estimates are substantially inflated, underscoring the need for reliable evaluation protocols in multi-LLM systems.

after.summary: Intensive care units (ICU) generate long, dense and evolving streams of clinical information, where physicians must repeatedly reassess patient states under time pressure, underscoring a clear need for reliable AI decision support. Existing ICU benchmarks typically treat historical clinician actions as ground truth. However, these actions are made under incomplete information and limited temporal context of the underlying patient state, and may therefore be suboptimal, making it difficult to assess the true reasoning capabilities of AI systems. We introduce RealICU, a hindsight-annotated benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) under realistic ICU conditions, where labels are created after senior physicians review the full patient trajectory. We formulate four physician-motivated tasks: assess Patient Status, Acute Problems, Recommended Actions, and Red Flag actions that risk unsafe outcomes. We partition each trajectory with 30-min windows and release two datasets: RealICU-Gold with 930-window annotations from 94 MIMIC-IV patients, and RealICU-Scale with 11,862 windows extended by Oracle, a physician-validated LLM hindsight labeler. Existing LLMs including memory-augmented ones performed poorly on RealICU, exposing two failure modes: a recall-safety tradeoff for clinical recommendations, and an anchoring bias to early interpretations of the patient. We further introduce ICU-Evo to study structured-memory agents that improves long-horizon reasoning but does not fully eliminate safety failures. Together, RealICU provides a clinically grounded testbed for measuring and improving AI sequential decision-support in high-stakes care. Project page: https://chengzhi-leo.github.io/RealICU-Bench/

after.summary: The rapid advancement of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) is increasingly accompanied by unauthorized scraping and training on multimodal web data, posing copyright and privacy risks to data owners. Existing countermeasures, such as machine unlearning and watermarks, are inherently post-hoc approaches that act only after intellectual property infringement has already occurred. In this work, we propose MMGuard to empower data owners to proactively protect their multimodal data against unauthorized LVLM fine-tuning. MMGuard generates unlearnable examples by injecting human-imperceptible perturbations that exploit the learning dynamics of LVLMs. By minimizing the training loss, the perturbation creates an optimization shortcut, causing the model to overfit to the noise and thereby degrading downstream performance when the perturbation is absent during inference. To further strengthen this defense, MMGuard introduces a cross-modal binding disruption, shifting LVLM attention to enforce a spurious correlation between the noise and the training target with theoretical guarantees. MMGuard is evaluated against nine open-source LVLMs across six datasets. Our results demonstrate effective, stealthy, and robust protection under white-box, gray-box, and no-box threat models, establishing a mechanistic advantage in proactively defending against unauthorized fine-tuning exploitation.

after.summary: A key capability for video understanding is reliably linking subjects to events across time, yet whether Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) actually achieve this remains unclear. In this work, we introduce DistractionBench to evaluate whether VideoLLMs can robustly link subjects and events in the presence of unrelated video segments. Through controlled interventions, such as inserting short advertisement clips into longer videos, we show that VideoLLMs frequently hallucinate interactions between entities from different segments, incorrectly attributing actions from injected advertisements to subjects in the main video. We characterize this systematic hallucination as bag-of-events (BoE) behavior, where models process videos as collections of events rather than temporally structured sequences. Evaluating 11 popular VideoLLMs, we find that all models exhibit substantial BoE behavior. Our findings suggest that VideoLLMs lack reliable mechanisms for temporal grounding and motivate the development of models with more robust subject-event association.

after.summary: Coding agents face new challenges in game development, where they must produce code that is not only syntactically correct but also consistent with engine-managed lifecycle, state, and networking behavior. Existing game-development benchmarks, however, do not combine assertions over engine-based runtime states with cross-client consistency, failing to evaluate how well generated code adheres to the desired behavioral specifications. To address these limitations, we present GameEngineBench, a benchmark of 110 C++ implementation tasks derived from 9 existing Unreal Engine 5 projects. Each task requires an agent to implement missing behavior within an established gameplay architecture. We also introduce Full-Session Verification, a testing framework that injects hidden tests after the agent finishes and evaluates the resulting implementation inside Play-in-Editor (PIE) sessions, with networked client worlds in 71 tasks. The tests evaluate Unreal's game loop, actor lifecycle, subsystems, and replication stack while directly inspecting runtime state. In 53 tasks, 119 tests additionally inspect a distinct client world to determine whether the authoritative server state is correctly replicated. To our knowledge, this is the first coding benchmark to evaluate cross-client replication. Across 11 model-harness configurations, the best-scoring configuration achieves 46.4% pass@1, while 43 tasks remain unsolved by every evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate that compilation and shallow verification overestimate agents' ability to implement behavior that remains correct during full engine execution.

after.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable zero-shot capabilities yet remain sensitive to real-world distribution shifts. Although significant efforts are devoted to adapting VLMs at test time, they rely heavily on noisy pseudo-labels predicted from cross-modal embedding similarities during inference, which are unreliable under distribution shifts and mislead the adaptation. Moreover, existing methods largely overlook the critical relational structures across different modalities during test-time adaptation, whose supervision signals remain surprisingly robust under distribution shifts. In this work, we aim to jointly align the cross-modal semantics and intra-modal relational structures across modalities at test time to improve VLM adaptation. At the inference stage, we formulate the zero-shot image classification task as a cross-modal alignment problem via a Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW) formulation, which considers both cross-modal semantics and intra-modal structures to generate robust pseudo-labels. At the adaptation stage, we propose a multi-level InfoNCE loss to leverage both the semantical and relational alignment supervision from the inference stage, empowering fine-grained adaptation of VLMs under distribution shifts with additional structural consistency. Finally, we bridge the inference and adaptation stages of our method by proving a mathematical equivalence between their objective functions, thereby revealing the mutual benefits of these two stages from a theoretical perspective. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our methods, outperforming the best-performing methods by up to 3% while maintaining a superior balance between effectiveness and efficiency.

after.summary: Exhaustively evaluating every candidate LLM configuration on every benchmark item to identify a high-performing one is costly. We formulate configuration selection as a cost-aware Bayesian bandit problem and propose GittinsEval, inspired by Bayesian-optimal Gittins-index policies for Markov chain selection. We augment this policy with a separate anytime recommendation rule over both fully and partially evaluated configurations, using an LCB-style score to account for posterior uncertainty. GittinsEval is computationally efficient, requiring only lightweight online updates after offline precomputation. Across tasks with varying numbers of candidates and examples, GittinsEval is consistently competitive, with particularly strong gains over the Bayesian optimization baselines on few-candidate large-example benchmarks and over cost-unaware frequentist baselines on large-candidate tasks. Crucially, GittinsEval often attains near-zero simple regret using only 1%-2% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost; it also offers a stopping rule that typically triggers at 1%-10% with an appropriate cost--quality tradeoff parameter.

after.summary: An agent can complete a task while exhibiting undesirable behavior during execution. Developers need tests for the specific behaviors encountered in deployment, beyond fixed benchmark suites. We present TraceDance, an agent system that constructs targeted benchmarks from deployment traces for user-specified undesirable behaviors. For efficient construction, Anchor-and-Confirm combines programmable retrieval with candidate-level confirmation by a Flash large language model (LLM), while the Anchor Synthesis Loop generates and revises specifications for custom behaviors. Nine frontier LLMs achieve a mean pass rate of only 26.7%, showing that they still struggle to respond appropriately at the evaluated decision points. Analysis across behavior-specific benchmarks further reveals weaknesses in how current LLMs behave as agents. By turning deployment problems into targeted benchmarks, TraceDance could serve as a key component of the recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop.

after.author: Woongyeong Yeo, Minki Kang, Chanuk Lee, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Sung Ju Hwang
after.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models (LLMs) through outcome-level feedback, yet recent approaches to finer-grained credit assignment often require auxiliary models, additional sampling, or privileged information. Although policy entropy provides a readily available signal, prioritizing uncertain positions under both reinforcement and penalization concentrates penalties where failed responses still retain alternatives for recovery, which can suppress opportunities for exploration. To address this, we introduce Entropic Advantage Policy Optimization (EAPO), an entropy-guided credit assignment method that treats success and failure asymmetrically. Specifically, motivated by the observation that success under uncertainty is less repeatable while confident failures tend to recur, EAPO couples normalized policy entropy with the sign of the response advantage to reinforce surprising success and correct repeated failure. It assigns stronger reinforcement to high-entropy decisions in successful responses and stronger penalties to low-entropy decisions in failed responses, while attenuating penalties at uncertain positions to preserve opportunities for recovery. By redistributing the response advantage across tokens, EAPO derives token-level credit directly from existing rollout signals without additional supervision. We validate EAPO on a range of reasoning tasks across both base and reasoning backbones, demonstrating that it achieves the best overall performance. We further show that EAPO promotes more effective exploration, broadening problem coverage and diversifying successful reasoning strategies.

after.summary: Looped language models separate computational depth from parameter count by repeatedly applying the same transformer block. Adapting these models requires a shared update that remains effective as hidden states evolve throughout the recurrent computation. Our empirical analysis reveals a pronounced late-loop bias in standard low-rank adaptation (LoRA): the shared update provides limited adaptation at early loop positions. This imbalance motivates training shared updates under varying combinations of their applications. Randomly omitting adapter applications alone, however, does not improve task performance; it reduces expected update strength during training while leaving inference unchanged. We introduce Loop Dropout, which couples stochastic masking of adapter applications with inverse-survival rescaling to preserve expected update strength and promote effective adaptation across loops. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved mathematical reasoning across model sizes, adapter ranks and training recipes, with benefits extending to general instruction tuning and code generation. Loop Dropout outperforms existing LoRA variants and adapter regularizers, while further analysis shows stronger early-loop adaptation. Every backbone loop remains active, and inference applies the adapter at all loops using standard LoRA without additional trainable parameters or inference computation. Code is available at https://github.com/NUS-HPC-AI-Lab/loop-dropout.

after.summary: Recent progress in large language model reasoning has been driven by benchmarks and reinforcement learning environments with automatically verifiable rewards, particularly in mathematics, code, and formal logic. These settings make model accuracy easier to evaluate and optimize, but it remains unclear how far success under fixed problem specifications and stable evaluation criteria transfers to reasoning outside such domains. Real-world reasoning often proceeds under incomplete and revisable information: conclusions may be supported provisionally, defeated by counter-evidence, reinstated by further arguments, or revised when stronger reasons become available. Reasoning of this kind is generally referred to as defeasible reasoning. We introduce ArgGYM, a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible training environment for structured defeasible reasoning. ArgGYM decomposes this reasoning into twelve tasks and grounds task-specific scoring in a symbolic argumentation engine that computes the formal states used to evaluate model outputs. It includes a frozen benchmark of 1,440 verified instances across fifteen curriculum configurations, two argument preference orderings, and two set orderings, while the same generators and verifiers can produce fresh instances, reducing dependence on static test sets, for both evaluation and verifiable-reward training. On the frozen benchmark, frontier and open-weight models show sharply different reasoning profiles: they can recover substantial parts of structured answers without solving the complete task, and performance declines in later curriculum configurations with longer dependencies and more interacting structures. Training Qwen3.5-4B with ArgGYM's verifiers as rewards more than doubles complete-task success on held-out instances, with the largest gains on constructive tasks.

after.summary: Evaluating an agent's ability to strictly satisfy diverse and procedurally complex requirements is essential to determining its practical reliability. Conducting such an evaluation demands agentic tasks that reconcile broad domain coverage with deep procedural complexity. Existing paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: expert-curated benchmarks achieve procedural depth but suffer from domain diversity bottlenecks, whereas crowdsourced benchmarks span diverse scenarios but lack execution rigor. To resolve this tension, we present SkillForgeBench, which leverages agent skills as unifying execution blueprints across three co-designed stages: (1) Resource Preparation uses domain-balanced skills to guide artifact retrieval, establishing broad workflow coverage; (2) Skill-driven Task Synthesis employs skills as procedural anchors to partition artifact roles, synthesize naturalistic task instructions, and package sandboxed scenarios for deep procedural execution; and (3) Holistic Evaluation Design translates skill-embedded requirements into fine-grained completion and process rubrics to enable strict requirement-level scoring. Comprising 842 sandboxed tasks across five major professional domains, SkillForgeBench reveals a steep capability hierarchy among eight mainstream agents, led by Opus 4.8 ($40.9\%$ strict completion). Requiring all constrains satisfaction uncovers severe capability bottlenecks across all model tiers that remain masked under individual rubric pass rates ($70.0\%$ to $85.7\%$ vs. $12.6\%$ to $40.9\%$). Crucially, under the external guidance from skills, top-tier agents obtain larger gains than low-tier agents (i.e., $\Delta 19.2\%$ for Opus 4.8 vs. $\Delta 5.8\%$ for Haiku 4.5). Finally, agents satisfy process rubrics far less frequently than completion rubrics (under $3\%$ for Haiku 4.5), proving that completion-only checks overestimate real-world agent reliability.

after.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable flexible parallel generation by resolving tokens according to the model's evolving predictability rather than a fixed left-to-right order. This flexibility, however, introduces training choices absent from standard autoregressive teacher forcing: which reference tokens are visible when a target is supervised and how much generation space is allocated. Standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) typically makes these choices through random masking, independently of inference. Our analysis shows how this training-inference mismatch can misdirect supervision. Random masking can conceal prediction errors or penalize uncertainty that decoding would otherwise resolve, while the attention-visible input length can change which response formulations the model favors, even when the underlying solution is unchanged. Motivated by these findings, we propose Predictability-Aware Canvas Selection and Supervision (PACS), an SFT method. PACS uses the model's own predictability to select each example's attention-visible input length and supervises reference tokens immediately before their confidence-guided revelation. Across reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, PACS consistently achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared SFT methods, with gains of up to 12.84 percentage points over vanilla SFT on individual benchmarks. Code will be released upon publication.

after.summary: LLM agentic workflows increasingly employ different models for specialized roles. Users may prefer different trade-offs between task quality and deployment cost, sometimes also considering latency. Finding good assignments incurs a separate search cost from evaluating multiple candidates. We introduce Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins), a multi-objective extension of single-objective cost-aware Gittins search for Pareto recommendation. It exploits the coupling between evaluation and deployment costs: assignments that cost more to deploy also cost more to evaluate. The search alternates between seeking higher quality and lower deployment cost, reusing each evaluation to inform both searches. After each batch, CC-Gittins recommends assignments that are nondominated under uncertainty-adjusted estimates of quality and deployment cost. We evaluate CC-Gittins on eight quality--cost matrices from workflows with two to five roles and up to 1,681 candidate assignments. We also evaluate the method with latency as a third objective. Across the eight benchmarks, CC-Gittins recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost, and recovers most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%.

after.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the match can be decoded from their hidden states. We trace where this information is lost in Qwen3-VL-2B/4B/8B/32B, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B on synthetic shape matching, HPatches point correspondence, and SPair-71k semantic correspondence, comparing input-matched probes with calibrated outputs. The models fail at two distinct points. Exact copies are compared and the result reaches the answer position, but the output does not use it, whether or not the shapes have names. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but are only weakly compared and never reach the answer position. The comparison runs through 16 to 32 attention heads that let tokens of the second image attend to the first. Redistributing their attention at fixed mass removes up to 32 points of accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads, and their attention is gated by salience and weighted by content. Training only these heads (0.02% of the parameters) recovers 25 to 28 points on SPair-71k and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. Unconstrained LoRA adapters, which reach higher accuracy, converge on the same heads: inserting only these heads' attention into the base model recovers 21-51% of an adapter's gain, mostly through changed inputs to the heads. Across all 14 trained arms, the selectivity of this small head set tracks the accuracy they reach, and it is read directly from attention, without probes or retraining. The gain in selectivity is not a by-product of more attention to the first image: it comes mostly from the wrong options no longer being drawn to the marked reference.

after.author: Adi Krishnamoorthy, X. Y. Han
after.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.

We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.

after.summary: Autoresearch agents, which autonomously design, run, and refine experiments, are accelerating scientific progress, particularly in AI research. However, existing agents rely on harnesses that combine multiple mechanisms, making it difficult to determine how individual components contribute to performance. We systematically study harness design for long-horizon, self-evolving autoresearch agents along two dimensions: context management, which determines what an agent retains from its past attempts, and skill management, which governs how it stores and reuses lessons from those attempts. Across MLE-Bench and KernelBench with gpt-oss-120b, gpt-6-luna, and gpt-6-sol, we isolate the effects of individual harness design choices by evaluating each against a recency-truncation baseline within a shared agent framework. items.content_text: In dynamic scenes---football matches, traffic streams, surgery, or assembly---actions unfold at fundamentally different time scales: in football, a kick happens in milliseconds, a possession lasts seconds, and complex events such as a successful pass followed by a goal combine multiple atomic actions over extended durations. Models trained solely on visual data struggle to learn effectively across different time scales, lacking a principled way of reasoning across fine-grained instants and…

after.author: Edjard Mota, Artur d'Avila Garcez, Maria Azevedo, Odalisio Neto
after.summary: In dynamic scenes---football matches, traffic streams, surgery, or assembly---actions unfold at fundamentally different time scales: in football, a kick happens in milliseconds, a possession lasts seconds, and complex events such as a successful pass followed by a goal combine multiple atomic actions over extended durations. Models trained solely on visual data struggle to learn effectively across different time scales, lacking a principled way of reasoning across fine-grained instants and broader intervals. Neither point-wise nor purely interval semantics suffices: the former fragments events into frame-level snapshots lacking overall event identification; the latter treats intervals as atomic truth-values, ignoring state trajectories. We introduce Temporal Logic Tensor Networks (tLTN), a differentiable neuro-symbolic framework addressing this duality via a formal, multi-sorted logic where events and states are structurally interdependent. Extending Interval Logic Tensor Networks (ILTN), tLTN grounds state predicates as fuzzy truth-value paths over time points, while events are first-class entities with learnable trapezoidal fuzzy durations and differentiable Allen-style relations. A compositional semantics fuses static, event-structural, and state-dynamic satisfaction into a single differentiable LTN grounding. Crucially, the modalities constrain each other bidirectionally: the interval layer dictates where point-wise constraints (e.g., Until, Since) are evaluated, restricting them to event-defined spans; conversely, the point-wise layer validates interval relations, rejecting them if underlying state dynamics contradict the relation. Through controlled synthetic examples, we show when single-modality learning fails and how this localization reduces frame-level computational cost on long traces.

after.summary: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) lacks a one-size-fits-all detector for heterogeneous data and anomaly types. Existing automation is limited by implicit objectives, potentially unreliable historical knowledge, or high computational costs. More fundamentally, it selects how to detect anomalies without explicitly defining what to detect. We propose SMAD, an LLM-based multi-agent framework that translates anomaly intent into executable, testable detection pipelines. Rather than selecting detectors against an implicit target, SMAD establishes a natural-language semantic contract grounded in measurable time-series properties, specifying target event patterns, expected score responses, and validation questions. This contract governs both detector construction and evaluation: LLM agents propose pipelines, while contract-matched synthetic interventions provide label-free evidence from the target series to assess semantic coverage and guide iterative self-refinement. after.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can now tune neural networks, yet without cross-session memory they spend costly trials rediscovering known lessons. Reuse is difficult because production models differ in architecture, training setup and inference budget. We present Engram, a memory system that links past trial outcomes with the hypotheses and rationale behind them and assesses whether this evidence applies to the current model. An online agent curates evidence at the decision points where it is needed: Initial Guidance supplies validated lessons at the start, Session Retrieval supplies related past sessions before each batch of hypotheses is generated, and Trial Candidate Review checks each trial candidate against matching past trials. Between sessions, an offline agent distills validated lessons, making the memory self-improving. On two ads models, Engram reaches the 32-trial result of a no-memory control with 47% fewer trials and also ends with a better model on average.

However, a one-time game benchmark can go stale as models, prompts, environment implementations, and evaluation policies change, and refreshing it is costly: full round-robin evaluation scales poorly in the number of model pairs, and the resulting outcomes live on incompatible per-game scales. We present a framework for continuous evaluation of LLM agents in game settings, organized around three coupled components. First, an adaptive scheduler that maps pairwise Bradley-Terry uncertainty to reduced per-pair match targets, concentrating budget on comparisons that remain unresolved. Second, a Unified Leaderboard (ULB) that reduces heterogeneous outcomes to pairwise evidence and fits a game-balanced Bradley-Terry model by minorization-maximization with bootstrap intervals, so that high-throughput games cannot dominate the aggregate ranking. Third, a game skill-profile methodology that scores each game along diverse skill dimensions, making the capability coverage of the suite explicit and turning game selection into a design decision rather than an artifact of availability. As deployed, the scheduler saved 61.7% of episodes; it counted each episode in the two team games as four records, overstating their savings, and the other eight games save 61.9%.

after.summary: Operational support is an important component of production software services. Support requests are often emergent and can come in many forms such as customer escalations or unplanned service interruption. Engineers across organizations have been successful in implementing automation to help streamline support processes but many solutions remain in the hands of human operators. A successful strategy to improve operator response times is to maintain up-to-date runbooks which are documents enumerating triage steps and remediation procedures in the face of identified incidents. This paper is an investigation into an operational system which incorporates Agentic AI into a runbook based incident resolution pattern. The bot uses information in the runbook corpus along with some system-specific tooling to guide the manual operator through the mitigation process then evaluate the outcome and suggest edits to the runbook where it found gaps and in its ability to triage the situation. By using the runbook as a medium to bridge humans and automation, the process maintains explainability and can be decoupled from the agent system. This paper demonstrates a collaboration between human operators and Agentic AI with results from an 17 week study involving 232 production incidents. We conclude with lessons on integrating LLMs into DevOps workflows, related work in AI-assisted operations, and guidance for reproducibility.

The v5 corpus contains 17 physics-based bug fixes, 16 process-representation modifications, 13 parameterization-scheme selections, and 14 parameter-optimization tasks. We define an eight-item patch-review rubric and audit five archived patch fixtures against the implemented local checkers. None of the five fixture diffs applies to its supplied starting files, yet three text-pattern checkers return a pass. A ParFlow expression replay disagrees with the reference slopes, and a MOM6 pattern check detects an omitted update. Inspection also identifies a retained VIC reference assignment that overwrites the intended vegetation-specific albedo. These findings expose limits of reference patches and local proxies as correctness evidence. The release provides a reproducible corpus and diagnostic tools; complete expert validation, comparative agent performance, and full-model execution remain unmeasured on v5.

after.summary: Jupyter notebooks support open-ended, multi-step assessments in which students build one logical flow across interdependent steps, combining code, written analysis, and generated outputs such as plots. These reflect authentic scientific practice but are hard to grade consistently, since students may make different yet equally valid choices at each step, so a later answer can only be judged in light of the choices a student made earlier. We present an LLM-based autograder for such flow-structured notebook questions. It generates a rubric from a reference solution, then applies a softening pass that relaxes criteria tied to the reference so legitimate alternative paths are not penalized. We report agreement, cross-model variance, cost, student perceptions, and injection resilience. With low-temperature models, agreement with human scores is often strong, including on the open-ended items the design specifically targets, while run-to-run stability depends sharply on the model's temperature support.

after.summary: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.

after.author: Zhe Chen, Emma Hsieh, Vicky Fu
after.summary: Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.

after.title: Internalized Experience: How Training Data Shapes Memory Formation in LLMs
after.author: Xianxuan Long, Xinnan Dai, Kai Guo, Jiliang Tang
after.summary: Parametric memory enables large language models (LLMs) to retain information from past experience and reuse it in subsequent tasks. Yet how training data supports the internalization of reusable task rules remains unclear. We introduce FSMem (Finite-State Machine Memory), a state-transition framework for constructing training data and studying how data content and organization shape memory formation. We evaluate rule reuse across synthetic worlds, classical planning, and code execution through valid-action identification and execution-outcome prediction, complemented by next-operation prediction in code. Our experiments reveal several systematic learning patterns. Under matched training conditions, even unchanged task rules become harder to internalize when learned alongside a larger variety of action types; by contrast, scaling the training data to provide broader state-action coverage generally improves rule learning. We further find that training at a single execution depth produces depth-specialized behavior, with models performing best when training and test executions have similar lengths. Motivated by this finding, we construct cumulative corpora that combine short and long trajectories, which can outperform long-trajectory-only training while using fewer training tokens. Together, these results demonstrate that the same task rules can be internalized differently depending on how execution experience is constructed, and that understanding these learning patterns can guide the design of more effective training data for parametric memory.

after.summary: Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. after.summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models because they can predict multiple tokens in parallel rather than generating tokens sequentially. However, recent studies have shown that MDLMs are vulnerable to backdoor attacks: when an input contains an attacker-chosen trigger, a backdoored model generates a targeted output, such as malicious code, while otherwise behaving normally. Despite this threat, backdoor defenses for MDLMs remain largely underexplored. We present UNMASK, the first defense framework for MDLMs that detects trigger-containing inputs, localizes the trigger tokens, and removes the backdoor from the compromised model. UNMASK exploits two fundamental properties of backdoor triggers, specificity and dominance, to assign a suspiciousness score to each input token. By leveraging two distinctive capabilities of MDLMs, parallel token prediction and token reconstruction at arbitrary positions, UNMASK computes these scores both effectively and efficiently. We further provide a theoretical analysis supporting the design of UNMASK. Evaluations across 40 settings spanning two attacks and four models show that UNMASK detects 99.3% of trigger-containing inputs at a 5% false-positive rate, substantially outperforming the strongest adapted baseline, which achieves 54.8%. UNMASK also achieves over 99% trigger-localization accuracy and reduces the average attack success rate from 95% to 1%, while largely preserving the model's utility on clean inputs.

after.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

We address this question by studying the performance of ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Ultra on a set of 100 open conjectures in geometric analysis. By construction, the model first selected open problems in geometric analysis that it assessed that it had at least a 50\% chance of proving or disproving, and then assigned a probability of success to each question. 13 questions were then excluded after an audit, and the model was asked to resolve the remaining 87 problems. The model was highly overconfident in probability magnitude but did more often than not assign a high probability of success to the problems that it did resolve, than the problems that it did not. Hence, its probabilities were numerically mis-calibrated but directionally correct. All proofs have been formalized in Lean, thereby verifying correctness, and have been run through a semantic equivalence pipeline to ensure semantic equivalence between the formalized and informal statements. These are exploratory campaign outcomes, not fixed-budget success probabilities. The certificates prove formal statements; for a couple of questions, some geometric inputs are assumed in the lean proofs.

Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.

after.summary: Skill-augmented reinforcement learning enables LLM agents to reuse task-solving knowledge across episodes, but existing systems typically expose agents to a flat skill pool and update skills only from coarse, episode-level outcomes. This conflates two distinct uses of experience: a stable strategy that should frame the whole episode, and tactical know-how that should be retrieved only when the agent reaches a local execution gap. We propose STRIDE (Strategy-to-Tactics Retrieval-guided skIll Disclosure and Evolution), a framework that brings progressive skill disclosure into agentic reinforcement learning. STRIDE keeps the selected strategy visible as episode context, exposes a compact tactic menu, and loads full tactic content only after an explicit retrieval action. This interface turns each retrieval into an event-level credit unit: the same event provides process feedback for learning when to retrieve and supplies evidence for skill-bank evolution. On ALFWorld, STRIDE achieves a 92.7% average success rate with Qwen3-4B and a 94.9% average success rate with Qwen3-8B. On WebShop, it improves over the strongest reproduced skill-augmented baseline by 4.5 score points and 1.9 success-rate percentage points. These results show that skill reuse is most effective when persistent strategies preserve global task structure and tactics are disclosed only at local decision bottlenecks.

after.author: Changyu Liu, Fei Zhao, Yiyang Liu, Xi Xiao, Tianyang Wang, Cheng Han
after.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks but often remain vulnerable to distribution shifts due to their fixed parameters during inference. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a pathway for dynamic adaptation, existing approaches suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to multiple sampling and the risk of error reinforcement from biased self-generated supervision. In light of this view, we propose RoTTT (Rotation-based Test-Time Training), a simple and efficient TTT approach that enables instance-specific refinement at inference time. For each test instance, RoTTT performs a small number of gradient updates by predicting the rotation angle of the input image. The known rotation angles naturally serve as a reliable self-supervised signal, enabling lightweight and stable adaptation without requiring additional annotations. Extensive experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that RoTTT consistently improves performance across different MLLMs, providing a practical and efficient paradigm for on-the-fly MLLM adaptation.

after.author: Kelsey Sikes, Sarath Sreedharan
after.summary: As with conventional AI agents, a common source of misalignment between Large Language Models (LLMs) and their human users is misspecified goals. Often, this happens when the human has skewed beliefs about the system's model and provides it with information that causes behavior different from what they expected, with potentially unwanted side effects. To ensure goal alignment, one solution would be for the LLM to ask the human questions about their objectives. However, it has been well-documented that LLMs most often provide default responses to user requests rather than try and ask questions to clarify their true intent. In this paper, we address these challenges by adapting a novel formulation for the objective misspecification problem to work with LLMs. We then test if LLMs that are prompted to ask questions about a user's true underlying objectives are better at identifying them compared to those that do not. We evaluate our method using four state-of-the-art LLMs tested on five standard IPC domains, showing that for some domains, asking questions greatly improved model performance.

after.summary: Multi-video understanding requires systems to combine evidence from different videos for cross-video reasoning. Answering such questions involves two kinds of decisions. Observation decisions must adapt to each video's content, whereas cross-video judgments require relating evidence from different videos based on the question. Most existing agents make both kinds of decisions in one controller, whose context accumulates observations from every video. We separate them in MVAgent, a training-free Multi-Video Understanding Agent framework with one LocalAgent per video. Each LocalAgent plans observations of its own video and keeps a private observation history. A GlobalAgent coordinates cross-video reasoning by instructing the LocalAgents and combining their reports with joint observation. We evaluate MVAgent on CVBench, MVU-Eval, and CrossVid, using three Qwen3.5 models of different sizes and GPT-6-sol. With Qwen3.5, our framework improves aggregate benchmark scores by 5.1 points on average over Single-pass inference with the same model and by 5.0 points over the strongest prior agent using the same model. With GPT-6-sol, the average gain over Single-pass inference with the same model is 4.3 points. On the same hardware, MVAgent also runs 1.8-2.7 times faster than prior agents of comparable size.

after.summary: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and $\tau^2$-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 $\tau^2$-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.

after.summary: Reusable skills provide specialized procedures, but large language model (LLM) agents must still determine how to organize and adapt their use. We introduce MetaSkill, a two-layer framework for reusing problem-solving methods across tasks and domains. The method layer selects from 26 curated methods and binds abstract roles to task objects. The execution layer uses the instantiated method to identify intermediate objectives, coordinate native skills, and guide repair or method reselection. On 89 SkillsBench tasks and 995 ToolHop examples, MetaSkill outperforms the evaluated baselines in all six configurations, with accuracy gains of 3.51-13.48% over the strongest baseline. Ablations support explicit method-guided orchestration beyond direct method injection and further gains from method reselection.

after.summary: Self-evolving agents improve by retaining feedback as reusable memories or skills, but every mistaken approval can shape many future behaviors. Two updates can provide exactly the same evidence to a verifier yet produce opposite safety outcomes, so the verifier cannot distinguish them from that evidence alone. We introduce DoppelVet, a verification framework that checks proposed updates before they enter an agent's persistent state. Without access to safety labels, DoppelVet constructs an alternative that matches every signal used by the existing verifier. It replays both updates from the same state and directly compares their behaviors in both presentation orders before deciding whether to retain the candidate. We evaluate DoppelVet on DoppelVet-Grid and DoppelVet-Tool, covering executable programs and natural-language memories. Across nine open-weight and proprietary verifiers, DoppelVet raises mean harmful-update detection AUC from 0.762 to 0.940 on DoppelVet-Grid and from 0.681 to 0.826 on DoppelVet-Tool, outperforming VaG and AgentDoG 1.5. On DoppelVet-Grid, it reduces trajectories experiencing degradation from 30.39% to 0.43% over a ten-generation self-update loop and leaves no final degradation.

after.summary: We present ChatNPC, a game companion that dynamically personalizes its responses in real time based on players' emotional shifts to enhance user immersion. The model integrates sequential data, leveraging the dynamic nature of streams to benefit from player information, spoken lines, and in-game context. We leverage recent progress in LLMs' tool-calling capabilities to extract vital information from memory and recognize potential constraints for accurate reasoning, thereby tackling the complexity of NPC conversation scenarios. The task is divided into a game sentinel-guided agent (SeGent), a memory capability, and a chat planning tool for reasoning instantiation. The approach uses a lightweight game template as an information framework, with relevant details and a thorough reasoning layout. We conduct extensive experiments on a newly developed game dataset for in-game context NPC dialogue and demonstrate that ChatNPC sequentially captures players' emotional shifts over time; responses are more naturalistic and human-like with appropriate conversational cues, pauses, and sighs; and utterances remain faithful to the dynamics of in-game context and player actions, supporting narrative continuity.

after.title: Layer-Level Control of Language Model Execution in Agent Frameworks
after.author: Ran Guan, Yiqi Lin, Xiangxi Tian, Yige Luo, Mi Zhou
after.summary: Agent frameworks typically orchestrate language models through prompt-and-response interfaces. We propose a harness design that exposes intermediate model states and layer-level execution controls to the agent runtime. By connecting state collection, policy fitting, and execution, the design enables policies to allocate computation within and across models based on intermediate states. We demonstrate the approach with a prototype that learns stitching bridges and state-conditioned execution policies from paired model states, then applies them during inference to select among continue, exit, and stitch. For dispatcher supervision, we select the least-computation action whose full-vocabulary next-token prediction matches the source model's full-depth prediction, using continue when neither early action matches. We train these components on a frozen proxy corpus of 5,000 typed-decision items authored using source texts sampled from WildChat conversations, then evaluate the prototype on JevBench measuring task accuracy, agreement with full-model predictions, and end-to-end latency including runtime overhead. Preliminary results show an approximately 15% reduction in mean latency while maintaining task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.
